tagline.text: An island of memory, etched with the tears and hope of Hansen's disease patients

items.credit: anne jimenez / CC BY 2.0 / Wikimedia Commons
anne jimenez / CC BY 2.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: A quiet island south of Coron, once home to the world's largest leper colony in the early 20th century. Walk through its museum, listed as a UNESCO Memory of the World, a church atop a coral-stone fort, and a hill bearing an eagle emblem laid in stone by patients, and reflect on a history of quarantine and healing.

Culion is an island south of Busuanga Island in the Calamian group, and also the name of the municipality that governs it. Combined with its 41 surrounding islands, the total area is about 500 km², with a population of around 24,000. It's just over an hour by boat from Coron town, but unlike Coron, crowded with island-hopping tourists, Culion offers a quiet village scene of a hilltop church, a small harbor, and pastel-colored houses.
The island's modern history began on

, when about 370 Hansen's disease patients arrived by boat from Cebu. The American colonial government quarantined patients from across the Philippines here, and Culion became, for a time, the world's largest leper colony. Patients were separated from their families and sent to what was called the "island of no return," and out of fear of contagion, a special currency was even created for use only within the island.

But Culion was not only an island of despair. Research into chaulmoogra oil treatment and drug therapy was carried out here, and patients built their own community, running a school, a church, and a band. Treatment concluded with multidrug therapy in the 1980s; in
the island left the Department of Health's jurisdiction to become an ordinary municipality, and in
the World Health Organization recognized it as having eliminated Hansen's disease. In
, the Culion Leprosy Archives were inscribed on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register for Asia and the Pacific.

Today, many residents are descendants of former patients and staff. This is a place to explore step by step, listening to stories as you walk through the village, rather than a destination of flashy sights, so it suits travelers interested in history, those wanting to add a different kind of day to a Coron trip, and anyone looking to rest in a quiet island village.

A museum inside the old research building on the grounds of Culion Sanitarium and General Hospital, displaying patient records, photographs, medical instruments, the island's special currency, and materials on chaulmoogra oil treatment. It's the starting point for a visit to Culion.
A hilltop church overlooking the harbor, its walls built from coral stone taken from the old fort. The contrast between the blackened stone walls and white trim is striking.
A coral-stone fort built in
by the Augustinian Recollects to guard against pirate raids. Part of the wall and some cannons remain beside the church, and the sea view from atop the wall is lovely.
A hill where patients laid white stones in
to form the emblem of the Philippine Health Service, an eagle. Climb about 330 steps for a sweeping view of the village, the harbor, and Coron Island in the distance.

The village layout, once divided into patient housing and staff administration zones, still stands, along with the old town hall, jail, and hospital buildings. Walking with a local guide lets you hear the story behind each building.
A marine protected area just off the village, with clear water rich in coral and tropical fish. Charter a bangka to combine it with a half-day hopping trip to nearby uninhabited-island beaches.

Culion doesn't have much lodging. The best known is Hotel Maya, on a cliff beside the church and fort, run by Loyola College of Culion, a Jesuit-affiliated school, as both a training ground for students and a source of scholarship funding. It runs about
a night, with rooms overlooking the harbor. Near the port there are a few fan-room lodges and homestays at about
a night. Rooms are limited, so it's best to contact ahead and book during long weekends and peak season.
Restaurants are simple too. Carinderias around the port and market serve home-style dishes like stewed fish, adobo, and sinigang for about

a meal, while the Hotel Maya restaurant offers fresh grilled fish and Filipino dishes with a view. Squid, crab, and seaweed dishes from the waters offshore are cheap and delicious. Many places close early in the evening, so it's best to have dinner early.
The museum mainly opens on weekdays and often closes over lunch. If visiting on a weekend or holiday, check ahead whether it's open.
Walking the village with a local guide lets you hear much deeper stories behind the buildings and records. Your lodging or the tourism office can arrange one for you.
The island has no ATM, or it's often out of order, so withdraw enough cash in Coron before you go.
Aguila Hill's steps are steep with little shade, so bring water and a hat, and avoid climbing in the hot midday sun.
For a day trip, check the return boat time first and plan your schedule around it. If you miss the afternoon boat, you'll have to stay overnight on the island.
Snorkeling gear is hard to rent on the island, so rent it in Coron or bring your own.
Cell signal is generally available in the village, but the internet is slow, so save your maps and boat schedule in advance.

Culion has been officially declared free of Hansen's disease, and there is no risk of infection for visitors. If anything, the stigma of being labeled a "leper island" has long been a wound for residents, so be respectful in what you say and do.
Don't photograph residents or hospital patients without permission, and move quietly within the hospital grounds following posted guidance.
The fort walls and old buildings are fragile, so don't climb onto the walls or remove bricks.
Crossing by small bangka is dangerous when the sea is rough. Wear a life jacket, and postpone your trip if the coast guard suspends departures.
In the marine protected area, don't step on or touch the coral, and use reef-safe sunscreen.
Many roads have few streetlights at night, so bring a flashlight, and come down from the hill steps before dark.
